To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a surveillance system for drug resistance in HIV was feasible in the European Union.

1) A steady increase in transmitted HIVDR has been demonstrated globally; 2) To support effective use ART and prevent spread HIVDR, monitoring of HIVDR is essential; 3) We piloted a European-wide surveillance system for transmitted drug resistance to assess the feasibility and challenges of implementation; 4) We conclude that standardised reporting of HIVDR was feasible in the nine participating EU countries, but legal barriers for data sharing and consensus on definitions and interpretation algorithms need to be clarified.

We conclude that standardised reporting of HIV drug resistance data is feasible in the participating EU countries, with the highest levels of resistance detected for non-nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor drugs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a surveillance system for drug resistance in the EU.
a pilot project to assess the feasibility and utility of a surveillance system for drug resistance in Europe.
the development of a surveillance system for monitoring transmitted HIV drug resistance (TDR) in the European Union (EU).

the pilot was successful in that it showed that it is possible to obtain information on HIV drug resistance at a European level.
the European pilot study on HIV drug resistance surveillance has shown that standardised reporting of HIV drug resistance data is feasible in participating countries.
this is the first study to assess the feasibility and acceptability of surveillance of transmitted HIVDR at the European level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the surveillance system for transmitted drug resistance is feasible and should be implemented at the European level.
the surveillance system was feasible in the nine participating countries and that the highest level of resistance to NNRTIs was detected.
the surveillance of transmitted HIVDR was feasible in the European Union, and that a European-wide surveillance system could be implemented in the future.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), in cooperation with the WHO Regional Office for Europe, is currently developing a European HIV surveillance system with drug resistance information that will be implemented by the end of 2020.

surveillance of transmitted HIVDR is feasible in the European Union, but that standardisation and consensus on definitions and interpretation algorithms is required for a European-wide HIVDR surveillance system.

surveillance for transmitted HIVDR is feasible at the European level, and that the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) is well-placed to coordinate and facilitate such surveillance.
